data.text/markdown:
Summary

A forecast product is a signal derived from a forecast that a downstream decision can use directly. A raw forecast says "0.8 kWh at 18:00 tomorrow". A scheduler, a trader or a grid operator usually wants something else: "will the asset be above its limit this evening", "how much energy over the day", "how much should I trust this slot". The model is held fixed (SeasonalWindowAverage, window=7: the simplest model that still gives a prediction interval), so the notebook is about what each product tells you, and what it cannot. Every product is computed from the point forecast and the 80% interval only, with no model-specific code.
  1. Daily energy, peak, ramp - the forecast re-expressed in operational quantities
  2. Uncertainty as an input - what the interval width says about each slot
  3. Event probability - the chance a slot exceeds a threshold, and whether to believe it
  4. Expected schedule - turning those probabilities into "high-load windows"
  5. From probability to decision - how much is at stake (expected exceedance), how cautious to be (a firm planning value), where to draw the line (a cost-based cutoff), and a replay of using them as metering arrives
Units: metering_kwh is energy per 30-minute slot, so a 5 kW load is 2.5 kWh per slot.

Section 0: Fixed model and base forecast

10 days train, 4 days test, one EV-charging asset. The model repeats one average daily profile (48 half-hour slots) across the test days, with an 80% interval around it. That is all the information the products below get.

Section 1: Daily energy, peak and ramp

||[E_{\text{day}} = \sum_t \hat y_t \qquad P_{\text{day}} = \max_t \hat y_t \qquad R_{\text{day}} = \max_t |\hat y_t - \hat y_{t-1}|||]What are these for? The forecast is 48 numbers a day. Most operational questions are about one number per day, or one number about shape:
Product Question it answers Who cares
Daily energy ||(E||) How much energy will the asset use or export today? Energy procurement, billing, battery or charger energy budgets
Daily peak ||(P||) What is the highest load we should plan capacity for? Connection limits, demand charges, capacity booking
Max ramp ||(R||) How fast does load change between adjacent slots? Balancing: how quickly generation or flexibility must respond
These are simple reshapes of the point forecast, so the real value is the comparison with what actually happened: a derived product has its own accuracy, which is not the slot accuracy. The table puts the forecast version next to the actual version for each test day.

data.text/markdown: Reading the table and plot. The forecast is the same profile every day: the 7-day window averages weekdays and weekends together. The test window starts on a Saturday, so the two weekend days (lower use) are over-forecast by roughly 40%, and the two weekday days (higher use) are under-forecast by roughly 10%. A sum does not hide a systematic day-type error, it accumulates it. Peaks fail differently: the forecast peak is the same each day, so it is too high on the quiet days and too low on the busy ones. The ramp columns show the same pattern: the forecast's sharpest step is the same every day, above what the weekend days did and below what the weekdays did. All three products are wrong in the same direction on the same days, because they share one cause (the model does not know the day type). For comparison the per-slot absolute error is about 39% (denominator floored at 0.1 kWh). The point is not that daily numbers are better or worse than slot numbers, it is that they fail in a different place, so each product's accuracy has to be checked directly.

Section 2: Uncertainty as a decision input

What the interval is. Besides the point forecast, the model returns an 80% prediction interval: it claims the actual value will fall between lower and upper about 80% of the time. The width ||[U_t = \text{upper}_t - \text{lower}_t||]is a statement of how much to trust that one slot. Narrow means act on the point forecast; wide means it is a rough guess. A downstream optimiser can use lower as a conservative planning value (assume the load is no higher than the 90th percentile, or the generation no lower than the 10th), rather than the model deciding for it how cautious to be. The question here is whether the width is believable. The two plots check the width against reality:
  • Left, interval width over the horizon. The model assumes error grows with distance: each further day adds one more seasonal cycle of error, so the width steps up at each day boundary (the model's ||(\sqrt{\text{cycles}}||) rule). Within a day it is flat.
  • Right, implied sigma vs actual error by time of day. The orange line is the one standard deviation the model applies to every slot. The blue line is how big the forecast error actually was, slot by slot, averaged over the four test days. If the model were honest about uncertainty the two would roughly agree. They do not: error is near zero overnight (the asset is idle, and easy to forecast) and large in the evening, while the model uses the same sigma at 03:00 as at 18:00.
What to take from this: the interval is too wide when the asset is idle and too narrow when it is busy. But the right-hand blue line averages over weekend and weekday days, and most of its evening peak comes from the two weekend days, where the model over-forecasts (Section 1): in this run the evening RMS error is about 1.1 kWh on the weekend days against about 0.4 on the weekdays, with the model assuming about 0.27 throughout. So two things are wrong, a spread that ignores time of day and a mean that ignores day type, and the second dominates here. Anything built on the interval inherits both, which matters in the next sections.

Section 3: Event probability

The idea. Treat each slot's forecast as a bell curve centred on the point forecast, with spread taken from the interval: ||(Y_t \sim N(\hat y_t, \sigma_t^2)||) where ||(\sigma_t = U_t / (2z)||) and ||(z||) is set by the confidence level (1.2816 for 80%). Then the probability the slot exceeds a threshold ||(c||) is the area of the curve above ||(c||): ||[P(Y_t > c) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{c - \hat y_t}{\sigma_t}\right)||]It answers "will this asset exceed 5 kW in this slot?" with a probability rather than a yes/no on the point forecast, which is the form a risk-aware decision wants. It is one probability per slot. 0.9 at 18:00 means about nine times in ten that specific half hour is above 5 kW. Averaging over the whole horizon, as the SARIMA notebook's Section 8 does, mixes quiet overnight slots with the evening peak and answers no operational question. Meaningful summaries are the curve over the day, the expected number of slots above threshold (||(\sum_t P(Y_t > c)||), valid without independence assumptions), and the windows where ||(P > 0.5||) (next section). "At least one slot above ||(c||)" is not computable from these, it needs the correlation between slots. Also, the SARIMA notebook divides the 80% interval by ||(2 \times 1.645||), the 90% z-value. ts_products.implied_std takes ||(z||) from the confidence level.

data.text/markdown:
Calibration of the event probability

A probability is only useful if it means what it says: events forecast at 30% should happen about 30% of the time. The table checks this. Every one of the 192 test slots has a forecast probability; they are grouped into bands, and for each band:
  • n_slots - how many slots fell in the band
  • mean_forecast_p - the average probability the model gave them
  • observed_freq - the fraction that actually exceeded the threshold
Reading it: a well-calibrated model has observed_freq close to mean_forecast_p in every row. If observed_freq is lower in the high bands, the model is over-confident (it says "almost certain" about events that do not always happen); if higher in the low bands, it is over-confident the other way (it says "very unlikely" about events that occur). The plot shows the same thing: points on the diagonal are calibrated, below the diagonal is over-confident.

data.text/markdown: What this run shows. The mass of slots sits at the two extremes: most are forecast as essentially never above 5 kW (overnight) or essentially always (evening). In the top band the model's mean probability is 99% but only 78% of those slots actually exceeded the threshold. The shortfall sits entirely on the two weekend days: there the evening slots were forecast as near-certain exceedances and often did not happen, while on the two weekdays every top-band slot did exceed. So the over-confidence is mainly the day-type bias from Section 1, made worse by a spread (Section 2) too narrow to admit it. The middle bands hold few slots, so their frequencies are noisy and should not be over-read. Practical consequence: use the probabilities for ranking and for rough planning, but do not treat a "99%" as 99%. A model that knows the day type, with time-of-day-aware uncertainty (e.g. quantile regression), is what would fix this.

Section 4: Expected schedule

The idea. Apply the event rule across the horizon: a slot is an expected high-load slot if ||(P(Y_t > 5\,\text{kW}) > 0.5||). Consecutive flagged slots form windows, which turns the forecast into "expect the asset to be charging 17:00-21:00". That is the form a scheduler consumes, for example to avoid starting a flexible job in that window. How to read the plot. Each panel is a calendar: one row per test day (the date is on the y-axis), and the x-axis is the hour of that day. A dark cell means "above 5 kW in that half hour".
  • Forecast - slots the model expects above 5 kW. The rows are identical because the model repeats one daily profile.
  • Actual - slots that were really above 5 kW. Rows differ day to day.
  • Agreement - the two compared: green = hit (flagged and happened), orange = false alarm (flagged, did not happen), red = missed (not flagged, but it happened), white = correctly quiet.
What you are meant to infer: whether the expected window lines up with when load really occurred. Look for the window being right in the evening but wrong at the edges, and for days (here the weekend) where it flags a window that never materialised. The count of each category is printed below.

Future idea: live schedule tracking (not built)

The agreement plot above is retrospective: the whole day is already known. In practice the same classification would run as actuals arrive, which suggests a small interactive app (Dash, or a marimo app with a refresh) for a chosen asset:
  • The user picks the threshold (the expected value, e.g. 5 kW) and the asset.
  • The day opens as the forecast schedule only: every slot blue where the model expects exceedance, blank elsewhere.
  • As each half hour completes, the live metering reading is compared with the threshold and that slot is coloured green (expected and happened), orange (expected, did not happen) or red (not expected, but it happened), with a marker for the current time.
  • A running tally of hits, false alarms and misses for the day, and the expected-versus-actual slot count so far, would show immediately whether the forecast is holding up or the day is departing from it.
This is the forecast product used as a monitor rather than a plan, and it connects to the residual-anomaly idea on the theory page: a run of red or orange slots is the early sign that the asset, or the model, has changed. It needs a streaming or periodically refreshed source of actuals, which the synthetic dataset does not provide, so a first version could replay the test days one slot at a time.

Section 5: From probability to decision

Sections 3 and 4 say how likely a slot is to exceed 5 kW. A decision needs three more things: how much is at stake, how cautious to be, and where to draw the line between acting and not acting. One product for each, using the same fixed model and the same 5 kW threshold. A replay at the end shows them being used as metering arrives.

5a. Expected exceedance: how much, not just whether

Two slots can both have a 60% chance of exceeding 5 kW, one by a whisker and one by a wide margin. If the cost is a capacity charge or a penalty, the amount over the limit is what matters: ||[E[(Y_t - c)^+] = \sigma_t\,[\varphi(d_t) + d_t\,\Phi(d_t)], \qquad d_t = (\hat y_t - c)/\sigma_t||]where ||(\varphi||) and ||(\Phi||) are the normal density and distribution. The result is in kWh over the limit, per slot. Summed over a day it is the expected energy above the limit.

data.text/markdown: Reading it. The table compares, per day, the expected number of slots over the limit and the expected energy over it with what happened. Over the four days the forecast expected 74.1 kWh over the limit and 54.2 kWh occurred. The bars show where in the day that exposure sits: mainly a morning block (about 06:00-08:30) and a larger evening block (about 16:00-21:00), which is where a mitigation (delaying a charge, drawing on a battery) would need to act. The daily columns show the Section 1 problem again: the same expected exposure every day, but the weekend days saw far less than expected and the weekdays somewhat less than their share. Quote this as a planning estimate with that known bias.

5b. A firm planning value: how cautious to be

The point forecast is the middle of the range. A commitment (a capacity offered to a market, a load you promise will be there to curtail) should be a value you will meet nearly all the time. Taking the 10th percentile of the forecast distribution gives a load level that should be reached or exceeded 90% of the time: ||[\text{firm}_t = \hat y_t + z_{0.10}\,\sigma_t \quad(\text{floored at } 0)||]The check is simple: how often was the actual at or above the firm value? The target is 90%. The right plot extends the check to every percentile: the nominal level on the x-axis, how often the actual fell below that percentile on the y-axis. On the diagonal the distribution is honest; the flat sigma from Section 2 shows up as a departure from it.

data.text/markdown: Reading it. The firm value was meant to be met 90% of the time. Across all slots it was met 74%, and in the busy slots, which are the ones that carry a commitment, only 53%. All of the red points on the left plot are on the two weekend days, where the model over-forecasts (Section 1); on the weekdays the firm value was never breached. A commitment sized from this interval would under-deliver when it matters. The fix is a better distribution (day-type and time-of-day-aware), or a more cautious percentile picked by running the check on the right-hand plot against history until the observed fraction matches the target.

5c. A cost-based cutoff: where to draw the line

Section 4 flagged a slot when ||(P > 0.5||). That is only right if a false alarm and a miss cost the same. Usually they do not. Say acting unnecessarily (shifting a load that was not going to breach) costs 1 unit and missing a real breach costs 4. Acting is worth it whenever the expected cost of not acting exceeds the cost of acting: ||[P \cdot c_{\text{miss}} > (1 - P)\cdot c_{\text{false alarm}} \;\Rightarrow\; P > \frac{c_{\text{fa}}}{c_{\text{fa}} + c_{\text{miss}}}||]so the cutoff here should be 0.2, not 0.5. The plot sweeps the cutoff and totals the cost on the test slots, to see how that theory holds up against the data. With a perfectly calibrated forecast the two would agree.

data.text/markdown: Reading it. Lowering the cutoff trades more false alarms for fewer misses. Moving from 0.5 to the theory cutoff takes false alarms from 12 to 23 and misses from 7 to 1, and total cost from 40.0 to 27.0, because a miss is four times as expensive. Going lower than the theory value buys little more. Treat the "best on test" cutoff as noisy: it is fitted to 192 slots, four days, and would move with a different window. The principled choice is the cost ratio; the data is the check.

5d. In practice: replaying a day as metering arrives

In operation the day-ahead forecast is fixed at the start of the day and actuals arrive every half hour. Each time a reading lands the question is: given what has happened so far, what should I do about the rest of the day? The replay below plays back one test day. Move the slider to change "now" (interactive when the notebook is run locally, the published page shows the default).
  • Realised slots are coloured with the 5c cutoff: green = flagged and happened, orange = flagged but did not, red = not flagged but it happened, grey = correctly quiet.
  • The rest of the day shows the forecast with its 80% band, and the orange shading marks upcoming slots whose probability is above the cutoff: these are the slots to act on.
  • The text underneath keeps a running score, and compares the overshoot so far with what was expected. If reality is running well above expectation by mid-afternoon, the evening is probably worse than the forecast says.

data.text/markdown: What this is and is not. The forecast does not change during the day: the replay only compares incoming readings with a fixed plan. That is already useful (a running score, a clear list of slots to act on, an early warning when realised overshoot departs from expected), but the next step is to let the readings update the forecast itself, for example by correcting the remaining slots for the error seen so far (an intraday update). The fixed model here cannot do that. See also the live app idea at the end of Section 4.

Findings

  • Every product inherits the model's systematic errors. The weekday/weekend blindness of a 7-day seasonal average shows up in daily energy, in peaks, and in the schedule.
  • Derived products have their own accuracy. Daily energy, peak and ramp need to be checked against actuals directly, not assumed from slot metrics.
  • The interval is only useful if its width is believable. Here it is flat across the day while real error is not (too wide overnight, too narrow in the evening), and the larger problem is the mean's day-type bias.
  • Event probability is per slot. Averaging it over a horizon is not meaningful; expected exceedance count and windows are.
  • Event probabilities are only as good as the forecast beneath them: slots forecast at 95%+ were observed well below 95%, entirely on the weekend days. Use them to rank, not to quote.
  • A probability becomes a decision with three more inputs: how much is at stake (expected exceedance), how cautious to be (a firm percentile, checked against history), and a cutoff set by the cost of a false alarm against a miss rather than a default 0.5. The firm P10 value was met far less than the 90% intended, because of the same weekend bias.
  • In live use the forecast is fixed and readings arrive each half hour, so the products act as a running score and a list of slots to act on. The next step is letting the readings update the forecast.

Not covered here

Baseline and response estimation, residual anomaly detection, portfolio aggregation, flexibility ranges and scenario generation. See the forecast products theory page.
